source: Torque on a Current Loop
A loop has magnetic moment μ = NIA, and τ = μ × B turns motors and meters.
Students think the torque is greatest when the field passes straight through the loop, where it is really zero.

A current loop in a uniform field feels no net force, but the forces on opposite sides need not act along the same line. Two equal, opposite, offset forces make a twist: a torque. That twist drives every electric motor and the needle of every old-style meter.

A flat loop of $N$ turns, current $I$ and area $A$ has a magnetic moment $\vec{\mu} = NIA\,\hat{n}$, along its normal by the right-hand rule (fingers along the current, thumb along $\hat{n}$). In a field: $$\vec{\tau} = \vec{\mu}\times\vec{B}, \qquad \tau = \mu B\sin\theta, \qquad U = -\vec{\mu}\cdot\vec{B},$$ with $\theta$ the angle between $\vec{\mu}$ (the normal) and $\vec{B}$.

Take a rectangular loop with sides $a$ and $b$. The two sides of length $a$ cut across the field and feel forces $IaB$ in opposite directions. Each acts a distance $\tfrac{b}{2}$ from the axis, with lever arm $\tfrac{b}{2}\sin\theta$. Together: $\tau = 2(IaB)\left(\tfrac{b}{2}\sin\theta\right) = I(ab)B\sin\theta = IAB\sin\theta$. The forces on the other two sides point along the axis and only stretch the loop. Since only the area appears, the result holds for any flat loop.

A loop in a motor. The torque is largest when the field lies in the plane of the loop and zero when the field passes straight through it; a commutator reverses the current each half turn so the loop keeps turning.
Worked examples
A 50-turn square coil $4.0\ \text{cm}$ on a side carries $2.0\ \text{A}$ in a $0.30\ \text{T}$ field. Find $\mu$ and the largest torque.
Moment and greatest torque
Largest at $\theta = 90^\circ$: $\tau_{\max} = \mu B = 0.0480\ \text{N·m}$.
The same coil is turned so its plane makes $30^\circ$ with the field. Find the torque.
An angle given to the plane
$\tau \approx 0.0416\ \text{N·m}$
The normal is $90^\circ$ from the plane, so $\theta = 90^\circ - 30^\circ = 60^\circ$.
$\tau = \mu B\sin 60^\circ = 0.0416\ \text{N·m}$.
How much work does it take to turn the coil from $\theta = 0$ (moment along the field) to $\theta = 180^\circ$?
Turning it over
$U = -\mu B\cos\theta$ goes from $-\mu B$ to $+\mu B$.
$W = \Delta U = 2\mu B = 0.0960\ \text{J}$.

"The torque is greatest when the field passes straight through the loop." That is where the flux is greatest, but the torque is zero there: the forces on opposite sides then pull straight outward along one line, with no lever arm. Check with $\tau = \mu B\sin\theta$: field straight through means $\theta = 0$ and $\sin\theta = 0$. Always measure $\theta$ from the normal, not from the plane.
